Image treatments

Every image needs an alt. Decorative images take an empty one, which tells a screen reader to skip them rather than read the filename.

Lightbox

A gallery tile is a thumbnail of something larger, and a grid that cannot be opened is a grid of pictures nobody can actually look at. Mark the collection data-lightbox and each tile data-lightbox-item, and the viewer does the rest.

Coastline at dawn
Market street
Harbor, late afternoon
Rooftops in winter
The long bridge
Orchard at the fence

Click a tile, or focus one and press Enter. Inside the viewer the arrow keys step through the collection, Home and End jump to the ends, the filmstrip jumps anywhere, and Escape closes. The art here is inline SVG rather than photographs, because the kit ships no assets — the behavior is the same whatever the src is.

It is modal, so it takes the whole dialog contract: the page behind it is made inert, Tab is confined to the viewer, and closing returns focus to the tile that opened it rather than to the top of the document — which in a gallery of forty is the difference between carrying on and starting again.

The caption is read from data-caption, falling back to the image's alt. The large image is given an empty alt on purpose: the caption beside it is already the description, and repeating it would have a screen reader read the same sentence twice.

Markup

<div class="gallery" data-lightbox>
  <div class="gallery-item" data-lightbox-item data-caption="Coastline at dawn">
    <img src="thumb-1.jpg" alt="Coastline at dawn">
  </div>
  ...
</div>

<!-- Point at a larger file than the thumbnail, if there is one -->
<div class="gallery-item" data-lightbox-item
     data-src="full-1.jpg" data-caption="Coastline at dawn">
  <img src="thumb-1.jpg" alt="Coastline at dawn">
</div>

The viewer element itself is created once and shared, the same way the scrim is, so a page with a gallery only needs the gallery markup.

Carousels

Arrows, dots and the left and right arrow keys all move between slides. Nothing advances on its own — an auto-playing carousel is a readability problem, not a feature.

Scroll-snap alternative

For a peek at what comes next, a snap scroller beats a carousel: it needs no script and works with a trackpad, a touchscreen and a scrollbar alike.

Embeds

Third-party frames go in a ratio box too, with a title so they are identifiable in a list of page landmarks.

<iframe title="…" loading="lazy"> 
<div class="ratio ratio-video">
  <iframe title="Product tour" loading="lazy"
          src="…" allowfullscreen></iframe>
</div>

Responsive images

Let the browser pick. srcset handles resolution, picture handles art direction and format fallbacks. 

<!-- Same picture, several resolutions -->
<img class="media-image"
     src="photo-800.jpg"
     srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1600.jpg 1600w"
     sizes="(max-width: 720px) 100vw, 50vw"
     width="800" height="450"
     loading="lazy" decoding="async"
     alt="Harbor at dusk, with cranes along the far quay.">

<!-- Different crops, and a modern format first -->
<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 720px)" srcset="portrait.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="landscape.avif" type="image/avif">
  <img class="media-image" src="landscape.jpg" width="1200" height="675"
       alt="Harbor at dusk.">
</picture>
lightbulb
Always set width and height. The browser uses them to reserve space, which is what keeps the page from shifting as images arrive.
